newsitem.title: USA: Senate panel to investigate Gulf War illnesses.
newsitem.headline: Senate panel to investigate Gulf War illnesses.

text.p: The Senate Veterans' Affairs Committee Wednesday hired a special counsel to head an investigation into the illnesses suffered by thousands of U.S. troops who fought in the 1991 Gulf War.
"We've got to get to the bottom of what went wrong. We've got to make sure this never happens again," West Virginia Sen. Jay Rockefeller, the senior Democrat on the committee, said.
He joined Chairman Arlen Specter, Republican of Pennsylvania, to announce that former U.S. Attorney Michael Rotko of Philadelphia would serve as special counsel for the investigation.
Specter said the committee had requested $1.65 million to fund the investigation. He said he hoped it could be completed in less than two years.
"The United States has a long history of mistreating veterans," Specter said.
As many as 60,000 of the 700,000 U.S. troops sent to the Gulf during the war against Iraq have complained of fatigue, skin problems, muscle and joint pain and other illnesses.
They have complained that the Defence Department and the Veterans' Affairs Department have refused to treat them or to admit that their illnesses could be war-related.
The Pentagon says it has found no common cause for the complaints, known as "Gulf War Syndrome". It says there is no evidence that Iraq used chemical weapons during the war.

But last summer, defence officials said they had learned that up to 20,000 U.S. troops might have been exposed to war gas when the Iraqi Kamisiyah weapons dump in southern Iraq was blown up just after the war.

Speculation on the cause of the veterans' health problems include reactions from drugs given to the troops to protect them from chemical warfare, pesticides, pollution from burning oil wells in Kuwait or a combination of these.
